note.note:
ENT Clinical Note – Telehealth Visit  
Patient: John Smith, 32 y M | Date: [visit date not recorded]

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure  
  • Recurrent unilateral pins-and-needles, weakness, and mild throat sensation during episodes; no identifiable food, drug, or environmental trigger.
- Symptom timeline and progression  
  • Episodes began 1.5–2 months ago; initially once per week → now several times per day.  
  • Each episode lasts ~3–4 days and then resolves completely.  
  • No symptoms during today’s call.
- ENT symptoms (during episodes only)  
  • Throat: “feel like there’s something in my throat;” denies true dysphagia or odynophagia.  
  • Voice: no change/hoarseness.  
  • Airway/breathing: no stridor, dyspnea, or noisy breathing.  
  • Swelling: none.  
  • Nasal/ocular: none.  
  • Ear/neck: none reported.
- Relevant past episodes / treatment  
  • No prior ED visits, admissions, or epinephrine/antihistamine use.  
  • No prior similar ENT or allergic reactions.
- Allergies and current medications  
  • Allergy: Penicillin (reaction details not documented).  
  • Medications: Aspirin 75 mg PO daily (self-initiated); no other regular or rescue meds documented.
- Social context  
  • Plastic-surgery doctor; lives with wife; non-smoker. Consult conducted from private location.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: none reported/visualised (video lost early in call).  
- Airway / breathing: patient speaking in full sentences; no distress.  
- Mental status: alert, coherent.  
- Vitals & physical exam: Not recorded (telehealth).  
- Third-party presence: none.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression  
  • Recurrent focal neurological episodes; GP’s primary concern – possible transient ischemic attacks (TIAs). From an ENT standpoint, throat sensation appears neurologic rather than obstructive/allergic.
- Evidence summary  
  • Unilateral sensory-motor deficits (hand, arm, leg) + transient throat sensation; complete inter-episode recovery; positive family vascular history.
- Differential diagnosis (aligned with DDx)  
  1. Recurrent TIAs – unilateral distribution, full recovery, vascular family history; episodes exceed 24 h (opposing evidence).  
  2. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis – age 32, days-long deficits, sensory + motor ± bulbar involvement; strictly right-sided pattern and high daily frequency are atypical.  
  3. Hemiplegic/complex migraine – young age, nausea; absence of headache and prolonged duration argue against.  
  (No ENT-specific pathology evident.)
- No transcript–DDx conflicts affecting ENT evaluation.

Plan:
- Immediate / urgent actions  
  • GP has completed urgent referral to hospital TIA clinic (target review within 48 h).  
  • Advise patient to call EMS/A&E immediately if symptoms recur and persist or if new speech, swallowing, voice, breathing difficulty, facial/lip/tongue swelling, or severe throat tightness develop.
- Patient instructions  
  • Remain accompanied when possible; keep phone handy; monitor for airway or neurologic red-flags.  
  • Continue current medication; do not start/stop any drug without medical advice (aspirin use to be reviewed by stroke team).  
  • Avoid driving/work requiring fine motor precision during active episodes.
- Follow-up  
  • Await TIA clinic appointment; GP number and TIA clinic/PALS numbers provided for scheduling queries.  
  • Consider neurology referral if vascular work-up negative (MS evaluation).  
  • No specific ENT follow-up required unless new upper-airway symptoms emerge.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing but expected:  vitals, detailed description of throat sensation (onset, severity), duration of each episode’s throat symptom, complete allergy list (reaction type), confirmation of alcohol intake, auto-injector availability not applicable but airway risk discussion minimal.  
● Transcript–DDx conflicts: duration (>24 h) argues against classic TIA; noted.  
● Transcript quality: generally clear; occasional audio/video loss limited visual assessment.
